message.content:
Below is a concise overview of the key rights and protections you have as a residential tenant in Texas. (This is general information and not legal advice; for specific situations you may want to consult an attorney or your local tenant‑rights organization.) | Area | What the law says | Practical Tips | |------|-------------------|----------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Landlords may charge up to **one month’s rent** for a furnished unit and **two months’ rent** for an unfurnished unit.
• The deposit must be held in a **separate, interest‑bearing account** (unless the landlord is a bank).
• Landlords must provide a written receipt and a **detailed itemized list** of any deductions within **30 days** of move‑out. | • Keep a copy of the receipt and any move‑in/move‑out inspection reports.
• Request the itemized statement in writing if you disagree with deductions. | | **Habitability / Repairs** | • Texas law requires landlords to keep the premises in a **safe and habitable condition** (e.g., functioning plumbing, heating, electrical, structural integrity).
• If the landlord fails to make necessary repairs, you may:
 1. **Notify the landlord in writing** and give a reasonable time to fix.
 2. **Withhold rent** (only after giving notice and following the proper procedure).
 3. **Repair and deduct** (pay for the repair and deduct the cost from rent).
 4. **Terminate the lease** if the issue is serious and unaddressed. | • Document problems with photos and written notices.
• Keep copies of all correspondence. | | **Rent Increases** | • For month‑to‑month leases, landlords can raise rent at the **end of each month** with **30 days’ written notice**.
• For fixed‑term leases, rent can only change at the start of a new term unless the lease itself allows it. | • Review your lease for any “rent‑increase” clauses.
• Ask for a written notice if you’re unsure. | | **Eviction** | • Landlords must provide a **written notice** before filing an eviction:
 • **3‑day notice** for non‑payment of rent.
 • **30‑day notice** for lease termination (month‑to‑month).
 • **60‑day notice** for lease termination (fixed‑term).
• Eviction can only proceed after a court order. | • Respond promptly to notices.
• If you believe the notice is improper, consult an attorney or tenant‑rights group. | | **Privacy / Entry** | • Landlords must give **reasonable notice** (usually **24 hours**) before entering, except in emergencies.
• “Reasonable notice” means a written notice stating the date, time, and purpose of entry. | • Keep a log of all entries. | | **Discrimination** | • Under the **Fair Housing Act** and Texas law, landlords cannot discriminate based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or source of income. | • Report any discriminatory practices to the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) or the Texas Commission on Human Rights. | | **Lease Terms & Modifications** | • A lease is a binding contract. Both parties must agree to any changes. | • Get any modifications in writing and signed by both parties. | | **Utilities & Services** | • Landlords must provide essential utilities (water, heat, electricity) unless otherwise specified. | • Verify which utilities you are responsible for in the lease. | | **Subletting & Assignment** | • Many leases require landlord approval for subletting or assignment. | • Obtain written permission before subletting. | | **Legal Remedies** | • If a landlord violates your rights, you can file a complaint with the Texas Attorney General’s Office, the Texas Commission on Human Rights, or a local housing agency.
• Small claims court can be used for disputes over security deposits or unpaid rent (up to $20,000). | • Keep all documentation (receipts, emails, texts). | ### Quick Checklist for Tenants 1. **Read your lease carefully** – note rent amount, due date, security deposit limits, pet policies, and notice periods. 2. **Document everything** – photos, videos, written notices, and receipts. 3. **Keep a copy of the move‑in inspection report** – it protects you from unjust deductions later. 4. **Know your notice periods** – 30 days for month‑to‑month, 60 days for fixed‑term. 5. **Respond promptly** to any landlord communication. 6. **Seek help early** – contact a local tenant‑rights organization if you suspect a violation. --- #### Resources | Resource | What it offers | How to access | |----------|----------------|---------------| | **Texas Attorney General – Consumer Protection Division** | Information on landlord‑tenant disputes, consumer complaints. | https://www.texasattorneygeneral.gov/consumer-protection | | **Texas Commission on Human Rights** | Handles discrimination complaints. | https://www.tchra.org/ | | **Local Tenant‑Rights Groups** | Free legal clinics, workshops, and advocacy. | Search online for “tenant rights Texas” + your city. | | **Texas Property Code** | The statutory law governing landlord‑tenant relations. | https://statutes.capitol.texas.gov/Docs/PC/htm/PC. | --- **Bottom line:** As a Texas tenant, you have the right to a safe, habitable home, fair treatment, privacy, and protection against discrimination. If you encounter problems, document everything, give proper notice, and seek assistance from the appropriate agencies or legal counsel.
